title: Acute angle closure and the acute red eye
subtitle: Painful red eye with blurred vision is never conjunctivitis

sources.title: Primary Angle-Closure Disease Preferred Practice Pattern
European Glaucoma Society Terminology and Guidelines for Glaucoma, 5th Edition
Clinical Management Guideline: Primary angle closure / primary angle closure glaucoma

red_flags.text: A painful red eye with reduced vision, haloes around lights, headache, nausea or vomiting, a cloudy cornea and a fixed mid-dilated pupil: acute angle closure.
Red eye in a contact lens wearer with pain and a white corneal spot: microbial keratitis, which can perforate within days.
Photophobia with ciliary injection (redness concentrated around the cornea) and a small pupil: anterior uveitis.
Deep boring pain that wakes the patient, with a violaceous hue and tenderness: scleritis, often with systemic disease.
Red eye after recent intraocular surgery or injection with pain and reduced vision: endophthalmitis.
Headache with nausea and vomiting labelled as migraine or gastroenteritis in an older patient: look at the eyes.

do_now.text: Suspected acute angle closure: same-day, immediate ophthalmology referral. It is an emergency that threatens permanent visual loss.

Start lowering the intraocular pressure while waiting, per local protocol: topical agents (beta-blocker, alpha-agonist, then a miotic once pressure begins to fall) and a systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, after checking contraindications.
Treat pain and vomiting; both perpetuate the attack and the patient's distress.
Do not dilate the pupil of a patient with a red painful eye and a shallow anterior chamber.

assess.text: Visual acuity in each eye, every time. Reduced acuity separates the dangerous red eye from the benign one.
Pupil: fixed and mid-dilated in angle closure, small in uveitis, normal in conjunctivitis.
Corneal clarity, fluorescein staining for a defect or an ulcer, and the pattern of redness: diffuse with discharge in conjunctivitis, around the cornea in keratitis, uveitis and angle closure.
Shine a pen torch from the side: a shadow on the far iris suggests a shallow anterior chamber.
Ask about contact lens wear, recent eye surgery or injection, trauma, systemic inflammatory disease, and recent medicines that dilate the pupil (anticholinergics, sympathomimetics, topiramate).

investigate.text: Intraocular pressure measurement by an ophthalmologist or trained practitioner. Very high pressure confirms the diagnosis in the context.
Gonioscopy and anterior segment imaging by ophthalmology to confirm closure and assess the fellow eye.
Corneal scrape and culture for suspected microbial keratitis, by ophthalmology, before antibiotics if possible.
Renal function and electrolytes before or soon after a systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitor.

resuscitate.text: Lie the patient supine while waiting. Check for asthma, heart block and heart failure before a topical beta-blocker, and for sulphonamide allergy and renal impairment before acetazolamide.
Hyperosmotic agents are used by ophthalmology when pressure does not respond to first-line treatment.

definitive.text: Laser peripheral iridotomy once the cornea clears, to relieve pupillary block, and prophylactic iridotomy in the fellow eye, which is at high risk.
Lens extraction is an alternative or subsequent definitive treatment in selected patients, decided by the ophthalmologist.

escalate.text: On-call ophthalmology immediately for suspected angle closure, endophthalmitis or a corneal ulcer in a contact lens wearer.
Same-day ophthalmology for any red eye with reduced vision, photophobia, a fixed or abnormal pupil, a corneal opacity, or severe pain.
Suspected microbial keratitis, uveitis, scleritis and endophthalmitis are treated by ophthalmology after same-day assessment, not empirically in the emergency department.
Primary care follow-up is appropriate only for a red eye with normal vision, a normal pupil, no photophobia and a clear cornea.

notes: Measure the vision. A red eye with normal acuity is rarely an emergency; a red eye with reduced acuity always is.
Acute angle closure is often triaged as a stroke, migraine or gastroenteritis because the patient complains of headache and vomiting. The eye is red and the pupil is fixed.
Treat the fellow eye: it has the same anatomy and the same risk.
